name: Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis)
populations: people after shoulder surgery or trauma
summary: A painful, then stiff shoulder from capsular inflammation, fibrosis and contracture, with marked loss of passive external rotation. The natural history is long and variable.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Long and variable; most improvement is early, and about 4 in 10 still have mostly mild symptoms at about 4 years

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Mainly an activity problem: return as pain settles and range and strength recover

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Passive external rotation restricted by about 50% or more compared with the other side, with a normal radiograph

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs to exclude other pathology; ultrasound or MRI only if a cuff tear or other cause is suspected

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Around 10% of people in their fifties; people with diabetes have about 5 times the risk

overview:
Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis) is a common condition characterised by spontaneous onset of pain, progressive restriction of shoulder movement and disability that limits daily activities, work and leisure [r1]. It affects around 10% of people in their fifties and is slightly more common in women [r2]. Biopsies from the rotator interval show a chronic inflammatory response with fibroblastic proliferation [r3], consistent with a thickened, contracted capsule.

The condition has traditionally been taught as three self-limiting phases (freezing, frozen, thawing) ending in full recovery. A systematic review found no evidence that people progress through phases to full resolution without treatment, and moderate-quality trial data showed that most improvement occurs early, not late [r4]. In a long-term survey (mean 4.4 years from onset), 59% had normal or near-normal shoulders and 41% had some ongoing symptoms, mostly mild [r5].

No single treatment is clearly best. In the UK FROST trial, manipulation under anaesthesia, arthroscopic capsular release and early structured physiotherapy with a steroid injection were not clinically superior to each other at 12 months [r6]. A systematic review and meta-analysis found that only intra-articular corticosteroid was clinically superior in the short term, particularly in frozen shoulder of under 1 year, and that it should be accompanied by a home exercise program [r7]. An older comparative study found that gentle, pain-limited exercise did better than intensive stretching [r8]. Explaining the long, variable course and matching treatment to irritability are central to physiotherapy care.

epidemiology.text: Frozen shoulder affects around 10% of people in their fifties and is slightly more common in women [r2]. In a long-term cohort of 223 patients, the mean age at onset was 53.4 years, women were affected 1.6 times as often as men and 20% reported bilateral symptoms, but there were no recurrent cases [r5]. In the UK FROST trial of 503 adults with frozen shoulder, the mean age was 54 years, 63% were women and 30% had diabetes [r2]. A meta-analysis found that people with diabetes were 5 times more likely (95% CI 3.2–7.7) than controls to have adhesive capsulitis, the prevalence of adhesive capsulitis in diabetes was 13.4% (95% CI 10.2–17.2%) and the prevalence of diabetes in people with adhesive capsulitis was 30% (95% CI 24–37%) [r9].

intrinsic: Previous frozen shoulder in the other shoulder (20% reported bilateral symptoms) [r5]
Other endocrine conditions such as thyroid disease are often reported as associated; evidence was not reviewed here
extrinsic: Shoulder trauma, surgery or prolonged immobilisation (secondary frozen shoulder). In the CSAW surgical trial, all six study-related complications were frozen shoulders [r10]
Reduced use of the arm because of pain from another shoulder condition (proposed contributor)
Upper limb or thoracic surgery and prolonged bed rest (proposed contributors)

mechanism.summary: Most frozen shoulder is primary (idiopathic): there is no single injury. A chronic inflammatory and fibroblastic process develops in the glenohumeral capsule, particularly the rotator interval and axillary recess, which thickens, scars and contracts so that the joint's capacity is reduced and movement, especially external rotation, is lost. A secondary form follows trauma, surgery or immobilisation.
sequence: A trigger such as a minor strain, immobilisation, surgery or a systemic factor such as diabetes (often none is identified) starts an inflammatory response in the capsule and synovium.
Chronic inflammatory cells (mostly mast cells, with T cells, B cells and macrophages) infiltrate the capsule and fibroblasts proliferate [r3].
The capsule, particularly the rotator interval and the axillary recess, thickens and becomes fibrotic, and the joint volume falls.
Pain is prominent and movement is restricted, most of all external rotation with the arm at the side, which is often described as the 'freezing' stage.
As inflammation settles, the capsule remains contracted and stiffness dominates over pain (the 'frozen' stage).
Gradual remodelling allows range to return slowly, although recovery may be incomplete and some people have ongoing mild symptoms [r5,r4].

variants.name: Primary (idiopathic) frozen shoulder
variants.description: Spontaneous onset with no clear cause, the form studied in UK FROST [r6].

variants.name: Diabetes-associated frozen shoulder
variants.description: More common in people with diabetes, who are about 5 times more likely to have adhesive capsulitis [r9]. Screening for diabetes should be considered when a person presents with it [r9].

variants.name: Secondary (post-traumatic or post-surgical) frozen shoulder
variants.description: Follows a fracture, soft-tissue injury or surgery, particularly when the arm is kept still. In the CSAW trial, all six study-related complications were frozen shoulders [r10].

variants.name: Bilateral frozen shoulder
variants.description: About 20% reported bilateral symptoms [r5]; the second shoulder often follows later.

anatomy.text: The glenohumeral capsule is a thin sleeve of collagen lined with synovium that passes from the glenoid and labrum to the anatomical neck of the humerus. It is reinforced by the glenohumeral ligaments, the coracohumeral ligament and the rotator cuff tendons. The rotator interval (the capsule between supraspinatus and subscapularis, containing the coracohumeral and superior glenohumeral ligaments) restrains external rotation with the arm at the side. The axillary recess, with the inferior glenohumeral ligament, is a redundant fold that unfolds in elevation. Capsular thickening and loss of this redundancy reduce volume and movement.

structures.name: Glenohumeral capsule and synovium
structures.role: Encloses the joint; the primary site of inflammation and fibrosis in frozen shoulder

structures.name: Rotator interval (coracohumeral and superior glenohumeral ligaments)
structures.role: Restrains external rotation at the side and inferior translation; the site biopsied and released in surgical series [r3]

structures.name: Axillary recess and inferior glenohumeral ligament
structures.role: Redundant capsule that unfolds in abduction; contracture limits elevation and rotation

structures.name: Rotator cuff and subacromial bursa
structures.role: Normally glide freely; compensate for capsular loss and can become secondarily painful

structures.name: Scapulothoracic joint and scapular muscles
structures.role: Substitute for lost glenohumeral motion, giving the 'shrug' pattern seen in stiff shoulders [r11]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
In 22 patients with primary frozen shoulder resistant to conservative treatment (mean 15 months from onset), biopsies of the rotator interval showed fibroblasts, proliferating fibroblasts and chronic inflammatory cells. The infiltrate was mostly mast cells, with T cells, B cells and macrophages, indicating a chronic inflammatory response with fibroblastic proliferation that may be immunomodulated [r3]. This is consistent with capsular inflammation leading to fibrosis and contracture, but the trigger remains unknown, and these were selected, treatment-resistant cases.

The functional result is a contracted capsule that limits the volume and range of the joint. Pain arises from the inflamed capsule early on, whereas stiffness dominates later. Because the capsule is the problem rather than the cuff or bursa, passive and active movement are limited equally, which is the key clinical difference from rotator cuff related shoulder pain.

structures.name: Capsule and synovium of the rotator interval
structures.effect: Chronic inflammatory infiltrate, proliferating fibroblasts and thickening [r3]

structures.name: Coracohumeral and superior glenohumeral ligaments
structures.effect: Thickened and contracted, restricting external rotation with the arm at the side

structures.name: Axillary recess and inferior glenohumeral ligament
structures.effect: Capsular folds adhere and fibrose, reducing joint volume and restricting elevation and internal rotation

structures.name: Joint cavity
structures.effect: Reduced capacity as the capsule contracts

structures.name: Subacromial bursa and rotator cuff
structures.effect: Secondarily irritated by altered mechanics and compensation; may muddy the clinical picture

muscles.name: Rotator cuff and deltoid
muscles.effect: Disuse weakness and sometimes mild atrophy with prolonged stiffness

muscles.name: Upper trapezius and levator scapulae
muscles.effect: Overactivity and scapular hitching (the shrug sign) to compensate for lost glenohumeral elevation [r11]

muscles.name: Pectoralis major and minor, subscapularis
muscles.effect: Protective guarding and shortening that reinforce loss of external rotation

muscles.name: Serratus anterior and lower trapezius
muscles.effect: Altered scapular upward rotation and control

cellular.timing: Variable; commonly described over weeks to months
cellular.description: Synovitis with a chronic inflammatory infiltrate of mast cells, T cells, B cells and macrophages, and fibroblast proliferation [r3]. Pain is highest.
Proliferating fibroblasts lay down dense collagen in the capsule, and the capsule thickens and loses its redundancy.
The capsule is contracted and stiff. Inflammation has largely settled, so pain falls while movement remains very limited.

cellular.timing: Variable; often a year or more
cellular.description: Collagen is slowly remodelled and range gradually returns. Recovery may be incomplete: 41% had some ongoing symptoms at a mean of 4.4 years [r5].

systems.effect: Diabetes is strongly associated: 30% of people with adhesive capsulitis had diabetes and screening should be considered [r9]. Thyroid disease is also associated (not reviewed here)
Chronic inflammatory cell infiltration and fibroblast activation in the capsule [r3]
Nociceptive pain from the inflamed capsule, night pain and, in some people, features of central sensitisation (proposed)
Night pain, long duration and loss of function affect sleep, mood and work; reassurance and a clear plan matter
Compensatory scapular, thoracic and neck movement can overload the upper trapezius, cervical spine and elbow

grading.system: Descriptive stages (freezing, frozen, thawing) — not a validated grading

grades.description: Increasing shoulder pain, often at night and with movement, with progressive loss of motion. Synovitis and early capsular fibrosis.
grades.prognosis: Often the most irritable stage. The idea that these stages have fixed durations is not supported by evidence [r4].

grades.description: Pain eases but stiffness is marked in all planes, especially external rotation at the side. Capsular contracture dominates.
grades.prognosis: Duration varies widely and many people improve earlier than the classic teaching suggests [r4].

grades.description: Gradual return of range with less pain.
grades.prognosis: Recovery is slow and often incomplete: 59% had normal or near-normal shoulders and 41% had some ongoing symptoms, mostly mild, at a mean of 4.4 years [r5]. Those with the most severe symptoms at onset had the worst long-term outcome [r5].

timeframes.summary: The course is long and variable. In a supervised-neglect group followed for 24 months, 64% reached a Constant score of 80 or higher within 12 months and 89% by 24 months, compared with 63% at 24 months in an intensive physiotherapy group [r8]. The classic idea of three fixed phases ending in full recovery is not supported by evidence [r4], so the phases below are descriptive ranges only.

healing.description: Increasing pain and loss of range; synovitis and early fibrosis. Variable duration.
Stiffness dominates, pain eases and capsular contracture is maximal. Variable duration.
Slow return of range and function; recovery may be incomplete [r5].

milestones.label: Pain begins to settle and sleep improves
64% of the supervised-neglect group reached Constant ≥ 80
89% of the supervised-neglect group reached Constant ≥ 80
Mean follow-up of the long-term cohort (59% normal or near normal)

timeframes.returnToSport: Not a fixed schedule. Return to normal activity as pain settles and range and strength return, usually over many months. Overhead and contact sport should wait for near-full range and restored strength.

symptoms: Gradual onset of deep shoulder aching, often worse at night and when lying on the affected side, with no significant injury
Progressive stiffness that makes dressing, combing hair, reaching behind the back and reaching a seat belt difficult
Sharp pain at the end of range and with sudden movement
Later, less pain but marked and persistent stiffness
Both shoulders may be involved, usually sequentially (20% reported bilateral symptoms) [r5]
signs: Passive external rotation with the arm at the side restricted by about 50% or more compared with the other side, with a hard end-feel [r6]
Active range of motion equal to passive range (both limited) in all planes, most for external rotation, then abduction, then internal rotation (capsular pattern)
Scapular hitching or shrug on attempted elevation [r11]
Normal radiographs of the glenohumeral joint (or the radiographs exclude other pathology) [r2]
Pain at end range, with relatively preserved strength where pain does not limit
Later: disuse atrophy of cuff and deltoid

subjective: Onset: gradual, with no or minor trauma; whether there was prior shoulder injury, surgery or immobilisation (secondary form)
Pain pattern: night pain, rest pain, end-range pain; irritability (how readily pain flares and how long it lingers)
Functional loss: dressing, hair care, reaching behind, driving, work and sleep
Diabetes (and control), thyroid disease and other systemic illness; contralateral shoulder history
Red-flag screen: weight loss, fever, past malignancy, chest symptoms, neurological symptoms
Mood, sleep, expectations and goals; previous treatments and responses
observation: Scapular hitching and trunk lean on attempted elevation
Protective arm posture (held close to the side)
Atrophy of supraspinatus, infraspinatus and deltoid in long-standing cases
Skin, colour and temperature of the hand (to screen for other pain syndromes)
palpation: Anterior capsule and rotator interval tenderness
Tender upper trapezius and levator scapulae (overload)
Subacromial and AC joint tenderness (to exclude other contributors)
rangeOfMotion: Passive external rotation with the arm at the side, measured with a goniometer and compared with the other side: the key finding [r6]
Passive abduction and elevation in the scapular plane with glenohumeral versus scapulothoracic contribution
Passive internal rotation: hand-behind-back reach level, and passive internal rotation at 90° abduction
Active versus passive: both reduced in frozen shoulder, in contrast to cuff-related pain where passive range is largely preserved
strength: Resisted external and internal rotation at the side, noting whether pain or true weakness limits
Scapular stabiliser strength once pain permits
Grip and elbow strength to rule out distal or neurological causes
neuro: Cervical screen: active neck movement, Spurling test and upper limb neurodynamic tests
Autonomic features (swelling, sweating, colour change) that may suggest complex regional pain syndrome
functional: Sleep position tolerance and night pain frequency
Disability and function scores (see outcome measures)

specialTests.name: Passive external rotation at the side
specialTests.purpose: Key diagnostic feature of frozen shoulder
specialTests.procedure: Patient supine or standing with elbow flexed to 90° at the side. Passively rotate the forearm outward to the first firm resistance. Measure with a goniometer and compare with the other side.
specialTests.positive: Passive external rotation restricted by about 50% or more compared with the other side, with a hard end-feel (the inclusion criterion in UK FROST) [r6].

specialTests.name: Shoulder shrug sign
specialTests.procedure: Patient actively abducts the arm and the examiner watches for scapular elevation and trunk lean before 90° of abduction.
specialTests.positive: Scapular hitching or shrugging to reach 90° of abduction. The test has been studied only once, so interpret with caution [r11].

specialTests.name: Capsular pattern assessment
specialTests.purpose: Support a capsular cause of stiffness
specialTests.procedure: Compare passive external rotation, abduction and internal rotation, in that order of restriction, and confirm a hard end-feel.
specialTests.positive: Greatest loss of external rotation, then abduction, then internal rotation with a hard capsular end-feel.

specialTests.name: Resisted tests and cuff screen (external rotation lag and drop-arm)
specialTests.purpose: Exclude a large cuff tear as a contributor
specialTests.procedure: Resisted external rotation and abduction at the side, then lag and drop-arm signs where range allows.
specialTests.positive: True weakness beyond pain-limited weakness, a lag or a drop.

clinicalRules.name: Diagnosis is clinical
clinicalRules.description: UK FROST defined primary frozen shoulder as unilateral shoulder pain with restriction of passive external rotation to under 50% of the opposite shoulder and with plain radiographs excluding other pathology [r2]. A meta-analysis found that no single shoulder test can be recommended as pathognomonic, so use the combination of history, range and imaging [r11].

clinicalRules.name: Screen for diabetes
clinicalRules.description: Diabetes is present in about 30% of people with adhesive capsulitis, and screening for diabetes should be considered at presentation [r9].

outcomeMeasures.name: Oxford Shoulder Score
outcomeMeasures.use: Primary outcome at 12 months in UK FROST (0–48, higher is better) [r6]

outcomeMeasures.name: Constant–Murley score
outcomeMeasures.use: Used to define normal or near-normal painless function (score ≥ 80) in a 2-year study [r8]

outcomeMeasures.name: Shoulder Pain and Disability Index (SPADI)
outcomeMeasures.use: Pain and disability across the course of care

outcomeMeasures.name: Goniometric passive range of motion (external rotation, abduction, internal rotation)
outcomeMeasures.use: Track the key impairment and relate it to the other side

outcomeMeasures.name: Numeric pain rating (night, rest, activity) and sleep disturbance

imaging.modality: Plain radiographs (AP and axillary or scapular Y)
imaging.indication: At presentation to exclude other pathology (UK FROST required radiographs excluding other pathology) [r2]
imaging.findings: Normal in frozen shoulder, or mild osteopenia; exclude glenohumeral osteoarthritis, calcific deposit, fracture, locked posterior dislocation and tumour

imaging.indication: If a cuff tear, calcific tendinopathy or bursitis is suspected, or to guide an injection
imaging.findings: Thickened coracohumeral ligament or rotator interval may be seen; excludes full-thickness cuff tear

imaging.indication: Atypical presentations, suspected cuff tear or labral pathology, or before surgery
imaging.findings: Capsular and axillary recess thickening, rotator interval changes; exclude other pathology

differentials.name: Rotator cuff related shoulder pain
differentials.distinguishing: Painful arc and pain on resisted tests, but passive range, especially external rotation, is largely preserved.

differentials.name: Glenohumeral osteoarthritis
differentials.distinguishing: Loss of passive external rotation with crepitus; radiographs show joint space narrowing and osteophytes.

differentials.name: Locked posterior dislocation
differentials.distinguishing: Fixed internal rotation, history of seizure, electric shock or trauma, and a posteriorly displaced head on the axillary view.

differentials.name: Calcific tendinopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Acute severe pain with a calcific deposit on radiograph or ultrasound; range limited by pain, not by capsular contracture.

differentials.name: Degenerative rotator cuff tear
differentials.distinguishing: Weakness and lag signs, with passive range usually maintained.

differentials.name: Cervical radiculopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Neck-related pain with dermatomal symptoms, positive Spurling or neurodynamic tests, and full passive shoulder range.

differentials.name: Proximal humerus fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Acute trauma and bony findings on radiograph.

redFlags: A locked posterior dislocation can mimic a frozen shoulder (fixed internal rotation after a seizure, electric shock or trauma, with no external rotation). Obtain an axillary view and refer urgently.

Unexplained weight loss, night sweats, past cancer, a persistent unremitting pain unaffected by movement, or Horner syndrome or neurological signs: refer urgently to exclude malignancy (including a Pancoast tumour) or bone metastasis.
Fever, a hot red swollen joint, or recent injection or surgery with severe pain: septic arthritis. Arrange same-day medical review.
Left shoulder pain with exertional chest pain, breathlessness or sweating: possible cardiac cause. Seek emergency assessment.
Progressive weakness, wasting or neurological signs in the arm or hand: cervical radiculopathy, brachial neuritis or myelopathy. Refer urgently.
Burning pain, swelling, colour or temperature change and allodynia disproportionate to the stiffness: possible complex regional pain syndrome. Refer for medical review.
People with diabetes: blood glucose can rise for several days after a corticosteroid injection. Advise monitoring and consult the person's doctor.

management.principles: Management is guided by irritability, duration, severity and the person's priorities, using shared decision-making. Explain that frozen shoulder has a long and variable course, that most improvement occurs early rather than late [r4], and that outcomes are often good but recovery can be incomplete [r5]. Intra-articular corticosteroid gives the most reliable short-term benefit, particularly in the first year, and should be accompanied by a home exercise program [r7]. In secondary care, manipulation under anaesthesia, arthroscopic capsular release and early structured physiotherapy with a steroid injection did not differ clinically at 12 months, so the least invasive and least costly option is reasonable first [r6]. Avoid aggressive stretching of an irritable shoulder, which did worse than gentle pain-limited exercise [r8]. Screen for diabetes [r9].

medical.name: Intra-articular corticosteroid injection
medical.description: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 65 studies (4097 participants) found that only intra-articular corticosteroid was statistically and clinically superior in the short term (up to 12 weeks): pain mean difference −1.0 VAS point compared with no treatment or placebo (95% CI −1.5 to −0.5) and −1.1 VAS points compared with physiotherapy (95% CI −1.7 to −0.5). The addition of a home exercise program was associated with extra benefit in the mid term. Early use in frozen shoulder of under 1 year was associated with better outcomes [r7]. People with diabetes need to monitor glucose afterwards.

medical.name: Manipulation under anaesthesia (with steroid injection)
medical.description: In UK FROST, manipulation under anaesthesia gave a mean Oxford Shoulder Score of 38.3 at 12 months, not clinically different from early structured physiotherapy (37.2) or capsular release (40.3), and had the highest probability of being cost-effective (86% at £20,000 per quality-adjusted life-year). Serious adverse events were rare (two with manipulation) [r6,r2]. Consider when disabling stiffness persists after non-operative care.

medical.name: Arthroscopic capsular release
medical.description: In UK FROST, capsular release gave statistically higher Oxford Shoulder Scores than manipulation (2.01 points) and early physiotherapy (3.06 points), but differences were below the 4–5 point targets for clinical importance, and serious adverse events were more frequent (eight versus two with manipulation) and cost was higher [r6,r2]. Reserve for selected people with persistent, disabling stiffness.

medical.name: Hydrodilatation (capsular distension)
medical.description: A meta-analysis of 12 studies found only a small effect on pain and range of motion (number needed to treat about 12) and a statistically insignificant effect on disability, with no clear effect of injected volume, concluding that the effect was small and clinically insignificant [r12]. The UK FROST report notes the increasing popularity of hydrodilatation despite a paucity of high-quality evidence [r2]. Not first-line.

medical.name: Oral corticosteroids
medical.description: A Cochrane review of five small trials found short-term benefits in pain, movement and function that may not be maintained beyond 6 weeks, with minimal adverse effects reported [r13]. Consider cautiously and avoid or monitor closely in people with diabetes.

medical.name: Screening and management of diabetes
medical.description: About 30% of people with adhesive capsulitis have diabetes, and screening should be considered at presentation. Optimal glycaemic control is a general health goal and may help recovery, but the effect on frozen shoulder course is not established [r9].

medical.name: Simple analgesia and NSAIDs
medical.description: Paracetamol and NSAIDs for pain and sleep disturbance, especially in the freezing stage. Choose according to comorbidities.

physio.name: Education and pain-limited gentle exercise (supportive therapy)
physio.description: In a prospective study of 77 patients followed for 24 months, supportive therapy with exercise within pain limits led to normal or near-normal painless function (Constant ≥ 80) in 89% by 24 months (64% within 12 months), compared with 63% at 24 months after intensive physiotherapy with passive stretching and manual mobilisation [r8]. This was a single comparative study, but it supports a gentle approach in the irritable phase.

physio.name: Early structured physiotherapy (mobilisation and graduated home exercise) combined with a steroid injection
physio.description: In UK FROST, up to 12 sessions over 12 weeks of mobilisation techniques and a graduated home program with a steroid injection gave a mean Oxford Shoulder Score of 37.2 at 12 months, which was not clinically different from either surgical option [r6]. It was described as an accessible and low-cost option [r2].

physio.name: Home exercise program of simple stretches and movements
physio.description: The meta-analyses found that adding a home exercise program with simple exercises and stretches (and physiotherapy) to intra-articular corticosteroid was associated with added benefit in the mid term, for example pain mean difference −1.4 VAS points (95% CI −1.8 to −1.1) versus no treatment or placebo [r7].

physio.name: Intensive or painful passive stretching and forceful mobilisation
physio.description: In the same 24-month study, intensive physiotherapy with passive stretching and manual mobilisation produced worse outcomes than supportive therapy within pain limits [r8]. Avoid forceful stretching, particularly in the irritable stage; aim for tolerable stretch that settles within an hour (a clinical convention).

physio.name: Electrotherapy (low-level laser, pulsed electromagnetic field, ultrasound, diathermy, TENS)
physio.description: A Cochrane review of 19 trials found low-quality evidence from one trial that low-level laser may help in the short term and moderate-quality evidence from one trial (63 participants) that laser plus exercise gave greater pain and function improvement than placebo plus exercise at 4 weeks. It was unclear whether pulsed electromagnetic field therapy and other modalities add benefit [r1]. Not a first-line treatment.

physio.name: Sleep positioning, activity pacing and heat
physio.description: Pillow support for the affected arm, avoiding sleeping on the sore side and pacing of provocative tasks; heat before stretching for comfort.

education: Frozen shoulder is a real, common condition of the joint lining. It is not caused by anything you did wrong, and it is not permanent for most people.
It can take a long time. Most people improve, but recovery is variable and slow, and some keep mild ongoing symptoms [r5].
Gentle, regular movement within comfort is better than forcing the shoulder. Pushing through severe pain does not speed recovery [r8].
A steroid injection can help pain and movement in the first year, and works best alongside a home exercise program [r7].
Surgery is an option if stiffness is severe and persistent, but the benefits over physiotherapy and injection are small and it has more risks [r6].
If you have diabetes, ask your doctor about glucose monitoring around any steroid treatment, and keep good general health habits.

rehab.overview: Progression is based on irritability and the person's goals, not on the calendar. The classic staging by time is not supported by evidence [r4], and in the irritable stage gentle, pain-limited exercise outperformed intensive stretching [r8]. In UK FROST, early structured physiotherapy consisted of mobilisation and a graduated home exercise program over up to 12 sessions in 12 weeks [r6]. Dosages below are common clinical conventions rather than trial-derived prescriptions. A 'tolerable stretch' is one that settles within about an hour.

stages.name: Settle irritability and keep moving
goals: Reduce pain and night pain to a level that allows sleep
Maintain comfortable movement and daily use of the arm
Explain the condition and the expected course
precautions: Avoid forceful or painful stretching in the irritable stage [r8]
Avoid prolonged immobilisation or unused arm positions
Monitor glucose in people with diabetes after any steroid injection

exercises.name: Pendulum swings
exercises.cues: Let the arm hang and swing from the trunk, not the shoulder

exercises.name: Supported or assisted elevation (table slide or supine with the other hand)
exercises.cues: Stop when the first firm resistance or pain is reached

exercises.name: Gentle assisted external rotation with the elbow at the side (stick or other hand)
exercises.dosage: 2 × 10 with 5–10 s holds, 2–3 times daily, within a tolerable stretch
exercises.cues: Keep the elbow tucked into the side

exercises.name: Scapular setting and thoracic extension
exercises.cues: Draw the shoulder blades gently back and down; avoid shrugging

progressionCriteria: Night pain mild (≤ 3/10) with sleep improving
Movements within comfort no longer provoke prolonged pain (settles within an hour)
Patient understands and can perform the home program independently

stages.name: Restore range (stiff phase)
goals: Regain external rotation, elevation and internal rotation
Resume daily tasks as range allows
precautions: Increase stretch intensity only if pain remains tolerable and settles within about an hour
If pain lingers more than 24 hours, reduce intensity

exercises.name: Sustained external rotation stretch with a stick (supine)
exercises.cues: Relax into the stretch; breathe and avoid shrugging

exercises.name: Wall slide for elevation
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10 with a 10 s hold at end of range, 2–3 times daily
exercises.cues: Slide up the wall, keeping the shoulder blade moving

exercises.name: Cross-body and sleeper-type posterior capsule stretch
exercises.cues: Hold at a gentle stretch, never sharp pain

exercises.name: Hand-behind-back stretch with a towel
exercises.cues: Use the good arm to draw the other hand up the back gently

exercises.name: Therapist-led mobilisation (graded to irritability)
exercises.dosage: As part of up to 12 sessions over 12 weeks [r6]
exercises.cues: Match grade and duration to irritability; avoid forceful techniques

progressionCriteria: Passive external rotation improving by at least 10–15° from baseline (clinical convention)
Elevation and hand-behind-back reach increasing session to session
Able to perform most daily tasks with minimal pain

stages.name: Regain strength and control
goals: Restore cuff and scapular strength through the new range
Return to normal work and activity
precautions: Build load gradually and monitor for flare in the new range

exercises.name: Side-lying external rotation
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10–15 with a light dumbbell, 3 times per week
exercises.cues: Elbow tucked to the ribs; slow tempo

exercises.name: Scaption raise
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10–12 with a light dumbbell, 3 times per week
exercises.cues: Thumb up, raise in the scapular plane

exercises.name: Row
exercises.cues: Squeeze the shoulder blades back and down

progressionCriteria: Passive range within about 10–20° of the other side in all planes
Strength ≥ 80% of the other side for external rotation and abduction
Pain ≤ 2/10 with normal daily and light work tasks

stages.name: Full function and maintenance
goals: Return to full work, sport and recreation
precautions: Increase overhead and heavy loading gradually
Seek review if stiffness or pain recurs

exercises.name: Overhead press
exercises.cues: Control the lowering, press in the scapular plane

exercises.name: Push-up progression
exercises.cues: Straight trunk; protract at the top

exercises.name: Prone Y raise
exercises.cues: Lift with the lower trapezius, not the neck

exercises.name: Daily maintenance stretches
exercises.dosage: 2 stretches (external rotation and elevation), 3 × 30 s, 3–4 times per week
exercises.cues: Keep the habit; early stiffness is easier to reverse

progressionCriteria: Constant score ≥ 80 or equivalent normal or near-normal painless function [r8]
Passive range within a few degrees of the other side
Full participation in work and chosen activities

criteria: Pain ≤ 2/10 with daily and work tasks, and sleep not disturbed by shoulder pain
Passive external rotation and elevation within about 10–15° of the other side (clinical convention)
Strength about 90% or more of the other side for external rotation, internal rotation and abduction
Normal scapulohumeral rhythm without hitching during elevation
Normal or near-normal painless function, for example Constant score ≥ 80 [r8]
Confident in the shoulder for overhead and loaded activities
tests: Goniometric passive range of motion compared with the other side
Hand-held dynamometry for external rotation, internal rotation and abduction
Constant–Murley score and Oxford Shoulder Score
Functional reach tests (hand behind back, behind head, overhead)

prognosis: The natural history is slow and variable. In a cohort of 223 patients followed for a mean of 4.4 years from onset, 59% had normal or near-normal shoulders and 41% had some ongoing symptoms, mostly mild (94% of those), and only 6% had severe pain and functional loss; the people with the most severe symptoms at onset had the worst long-term prognosis [r5]. A systematic review found low-quality evidence that untreated shoulders improved in range, but incompletely, over 1 to 4 years, and moderate-quality evidence that most improvement occurs early [r4]. In UK FROST at 12 months, mean Oxford Shoulder Scores were 37.2 to 40.3 across three treatment arms, with no clinically important differences [r6]. Recurrence in the same shoulder was not seen, but 20% had bilateral symptoms [r5]. Diabetes is a risk factor for developing frozen shoulder [r9]; whether it worsens prognosis was not established in the sources reviewed.
prevention: No intervention has been shown to prevent primary frozen shoulder
After shoulder injury or surgery, encourage early, comfortable movement and avoid prolonged immobilisation (a reasonable principle; evidence is limited)
Seek early assessment for new shoulder pain with loss of movement so that treatment can start in the first year, when intra-articular steroid appears most helpful [r7]
clinicalPearls: Test passive external rotation at the side first. Frozen shoulder shows a marked loss (restriction of about 50% or more compared with the other side was the UK FROST criterion) with a normal radiograph; if passive external rotation is near-normal, think of cuff-related pain or another cause [r6].
Do not promise a fixed 18-month course. The three-phase model is not supported by evidence, most improvement comes early, and a minority have ongoing symptoms [r4,r5].
Match intensity to irritability. In the irritable stage, gentle pain-limited exercise did better than intensive stretching [r8].
Consider an early steroid injection with a home exercise program if the shoulder has been stiff for under a year [r7].
Screen for diabetes at presentation [r9], and warn diabetic patients about glucose rises after an injection.
A stiff shoulder after arthroscopic surgery is a recognised complication: all six study-related complications in the CSAW trial were frozen shoulders [r10].

captions.text: There is usually no single injury: over weeks the shoulder becomes painful and then stiff.
Reaching up becomes difficult, and the person leans and shrugs to compensate.
Movement is blocked, especially outward rotation, even when someone else moves the arm.
Zooming into the right shoulder to see the joint capsule.
The capsule is a thin sleeve of collagen that lets the joint move freely in all directions.
In frozen shoulder it becomes inflamed, and the lining is thick and painful.
Fibroblasts lay down dense scar, and the capsule and ligaments thicken.
The capsule tightens, the joint space shrinks, and external rotation is lost.
Pain eases but the shoulder stays stiff in all planes.
Over months to years the capsule slowly remodels and range returns, although recovery can be incomplete.
Healthy capsule: a thin synovial lining over loosely woven collagen.
Inflammation: mast cells, T cells and macrophages infiltrate and fibroblasts multiply.
Fibrosis: dense collagen is laid down and the capsule thickens.
Contracture: the scarred capsule is short and stiff, limiting range.
Remodelling: collagen reorganises slowly and range gradually returns.
